\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, entity voting provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$, Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), though exact match leads binary discrimination on SciERC (AUROC${=}0.749$).
When temperature or cross-condition robustness is required, SJ is preferable: its temperature sensitivity is small with bootstrap CIs including zero (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}).
Under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$), extending binary-agreement advantages to the within-capability regime.
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: EM dominates on easy tasks (CoNLL, F1${>}$0.91), Voting and SJ dominate on hard tasks (SciERC, F1$\,{\approx}\,$0.66), and all signals converge when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17).
This ordering is consistent across tested model families, suggesting the difficulty gradient determines which signal family is most informative.
Conditional filtering confirms this pattern: removing zero-F1 instances shifts effective difficulty toward the easy-task regime, and EM reclaims the lead while Voting and SJ drop substantially (Voting RE: $0.350{\to}0.241$).
While our NER findings are validated across three datasets, our RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone and warrant further validation.

\paragraph{Why quality estimators fail as selectors.}
The four instance-level signals (Voting, SJ, FK, EM) produce a single score per input, which by construction cannot rank $N$ candidates; the consensus-proximity strategy (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) converts them to per-sample scores, but the resulting selection performance (Table~\ref{tab:selection}) shows this conversion adds no reliable value.
Quality estimation ranks \textit{instances} by expected output quality; sample selection ranks \textit{candidates within a single instance}, requiring per-sample quality information that instance-level aggregation discards.
On SciERC NER, the random baseline (0.608) falls 3.6~pp below greedy (0.644), confirming per-instance sample variance exists; yet the oracle gap of 13.2~pp shows substantially better candidates exist, and the best signal captures only +0.6~pp ($p{=}0.39$).
We observe a notable $\rho$--AUROC dissociation: on SciERC, EM achieves AUROC of 0.749 (NER) and 0.706 (RE) yet ranks third or last in $\rho$, because EM${=}1$ collapses both all-correct and all-wrong instances into the same binary outcome, destroying rank order while preserving discriminative power (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).
The practical implication is that these signals are well-suited for routing and triage---flagging uncertain instances for human review---but not for fine-grained ranking within a difficulty tier.

\paragraph{Why logprob fails as a selector.}
Log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---also fails at selection despite its structural advantage for candidate ranking.
Under constrained decoding, logprob primarily reflects grammar compliance rather than semantic extraction quality: a sample may have high token-level confidence yet extract the wrong relation arguments.
Bootstrap analysis reveals that 75\% of instance-level logprob comparisons are effectively ties (win\%${=}$46.6\%, comparable to random), consistent with the non-significant selection result ($p{=}0.39$).
NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (ECE 0.069--0.096), but RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) suggests that logprob confidence scores are poorly aligned with extraction quality for compound tasks.
Constrained decoding enforces schema compliance at the token level, which may compress per-sample diversity beyond what free-form generation would exhibit.
The random baseline gap (3.6~pp) confirms meaningful variance exists even under constraints, but the correlation-selection gap may partially reflect this reduced diversity.
Future work should compare constrained vs.\ unconstrained decoding to disentangle these effects.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means that evaluating confidence signals on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective best-of-$N$ selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} that can evaluate individual outputs rather than distribution-level properties.
Further $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows that $N{=}8$ captures most achievable quality estimation benefit; additional samples widen the correlation-selection gap absent stronger selectors.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time scaling through multi-sample generation promises quality improvements for LLM-based information extraction, but which confidence signals best serve quality estimation versus sample selection remains unclear.
3	We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER and relation extraction on three datasets (SciERC, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17) with two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B).
4	We find that the strongest signals achieve $\rho{=}0.38$ (entity voting) and AUROC${=}0.75$ (exact match) for quality estimation, with ranking and classification favoring different signals across task complexity; however, this strong quality estimation does not translate into selection gains---no signal reliably surpasses greedy decoding on either task ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
